title: Unique identifier linking across contexts
description: During account registration and device enrollment, the Home Hub processes unique identifiers (email, username, device IDs) that can be used to link the homeowner's data across different contexts or services.
assumptions: Registration requires unique identifiers for account and device management

title: Profiling through device enrollment patterns
description: The Home Hub can analyze which cameras/sensors are enrolled and their configuration to create a profile of the homeowner's security preferences, home layout, and lifestyle patterns.
assumptions: Device enrollment data includes device types, locations, and settings

title: Processing of identified data during registration
description: The Home Hub requests and processes identified personal data from the homeowner during account registration, including name, contact information, and potentially payment details.
assumptions: Account registration requires personally identifiable information

title: Device identifiers as unique references
description: Camera and sensor device IDs processed during enrollment serve as unique references that can be linked back to the specific homeowner and their property.
assumptions: Devices have unique serial numbers or identifiers

title: Registration data prevents deniability
description: Account registration and device enrollment records create attributable data evidence that can prevent the homeowner from denying their association with the system or specific devices.
assumptions: Registration creates persistent records with timestamps

title: Registration communications observable
description: The data flow during account registration and device enrollment could be observed by network monitors, revealing that a registration event occurred and potentially metadata about the devices being enrolled.
assumptions: Registration traffic traverses network infrastructure

title: Potentially excessive data type sensitivity
description: Account registration may collect more sensitive data types than functionally required, such as detailed contact information, payment data, or home address beyond what's needed for basic device enrollment.
assumptions: Registration form may request more data than minimally necessary

title: Data retention beyond functional need
description: Registration and enrollment data may be retained longer than functionally necessary for the stated purpose of device management, potentially indefinitely without clear retention policies.
assumptions: No explicit retention policy mentioned for registration data

title: Unawareness of data processing scope
description: Homeowners may not be fully aware of all the personal data being collected, how it will be processed, stored, or potentially shared during the registration and enrollment process.
assumptions: Privacy notices may not clearly explain all processing activities

title: Limited control over data processing preferences
description: Homeowners may lack meaningful control to set preferences or consent choices regarding how their registration and device enrollment data is processed, stored, or used.
assumptions: Registration process may not offer granular consent options

title: Potential violation of data minimization principle
description: If the Home Hub collects more personal data during registration than is strictly necessary for device enrollment and account management, this could violate GDPR's data minimization principle.
assumptions: Registration may collect data beyond functional requirements
uncertainty_note: Depends on actual data collection practices

title: Guest access code linked to individual
description: The temporary access code entered by the guest may be unique to that guest or session. If the Home Hub logs which code was used and when, this creates a link between the guest and the access event, potentially enabling tracking of guest movements and access patterns.
assumptions: The Home Hub maintains logs of access codes used and timestamps

title: Access code serves as guest identifier
description: If the temporary access code is unique to a specific guest, it functions as an identifier that can be used to identify the data subject. The Home Hub processing this code could enable identification of which guest accessed the property.
assumptions: The access code is unique per guest or guest session

title: Access event attributable to guest
description: The access code entry creates a data record that can be attributed to the guest, preventing them from denying they accessed the property. The Home Hub's logging of the code and unlock event provides evidence of the guest's action.
assumptions: The Home Hub logs access code entries and door unlock events

title: Access code retained longer than necessary
description: If the Home Hub retains the temporary access code or associated logs longer than needed for the access control function, this violates data minimization principles. Temporary codes should be invalidated and deleted promptly after use.
assumptions: The Home Hub may store access logs beyond the immediate access event

title: Guest unaware of data processing
description: The guest may not be aware that their access code entry is being logged, stored, or processed by the Home Hub beyond the immediate door unlock function. They may not know what data is collected or how long it is retained.
assumptions: No clear notification is provided to guests about data processing

title: Violation of data minimization principle
description: If the Home Hub collects or retains more data than necessary (e.g., storing access codes longer than needed, logging unnecessary metadata), this may violate GDPR's data minimization principle requiring processing to be adequate, relevant, and limited to what is necessary.
assumptions: The system may process or store data beyond functional requirements

title: Sensitive behavioral data collection
description: Motion, door, and sensor events reveal presence, movement patterns, and behavior of individuals in the home, which constitutes sensitive personal data that should only be collected when strictly required.
assumptions: Sensor events can reveal when individuals are present, which rooms they occupy, and their daily routines.

title: Behavioral profiling through sensor data
description: Stored sensor events can be analyzed to create behavioral profiles of individuals, linking data to specific individuals based on their movement and activity patterns.
assumptions: Event log data can be queried and analyzed to identify patterns in individual behavior over time.

title: Quasi-identifier through sensor data combinations
description: Combinations of sensor attributes (which door, timing, motion patterns) can serve as quasi-identifiers that uniquely identify individuals within the household.
assumptions: Multiple sensor data points can be combined to distinguish between different individuals.

title: Excessive data retention in event log
description: Sensor event data may be retained in the local event log longer than functionally needed for the system's purposes.
assumptions: Event logs typically retain data for extended periods without automatic deletion policies.

title: Unawareness of sensor data collection
description: Residents may not be aware that their motion, door, and sensor events are being collected and logged by the Home Hub.
assumptions: Sensor data collection may occur without explicit notification or consent from data subjects.

title: Lack of control over sensor data erasure
description: Data subjects may lack control to rectify or erase their sensor event data from the local event log.
assumptions: Event logs may not provide mechanisms for individuals to request deletion of their data.

title: Event log as attributable evidence
description: Sensor event data in the log can be used as evidence to attribute actions or presence to specific individuals, preventing deniability.
assumptions: Event timestamps and sensor locations can be used to establish when and where individuals were present.

title: Violation of data minimization principle
description: The Home Hub may collect more sensor data than is actually needed for its functional purposes, violating GDPR data minimization requirements.
assumptions: All sensor events are logged without filtering for functional necessity.

title: Violation of storage limitation principle
description: Sensor event data may be stored in the event log longer than necessary, violating GDPR storage limitation requirements.
assumptions: No automatic retention policies or deletion mechanisms are in place for the event log.

title: Sensitive video data uploaded
description: Home Hub uploads recorded camera clips which are highly sensitive personal data types containing visual information about individuals, their activities, and locations. This exceeds what might be functionally required depending on the use case.
assumptions: Video clips contain personally identifiable visual information

title: Processing of identified data in video storage
description: Cloud video storage processes video clips that contain identified information such as faces, license plates, and other visual identifiers that can directly identify data subjects.
assumptions: Video content contains identifiable visual information

title: Profiling through video analysis
description: Stored video clips can be analyzed to profile individuals based on their activities, movements, behaviors, and patterns over time, enabling linking of data to specific individuals.
assumptions: Cloud storage or associated services may analyze video content for patterns

title: Video as attributable evidence
description: Stored video clips can be used as data evidence to prevent individuals from denying certain claims about their presence, activities, or actions at specific times and locations.
assumptions: Video content can serve as evidentiary material

title: Detection through observed communications
description: The data flow of uploading video clips to cloud storage can be detected through network monitoring, revealing that video data transfer is occurring between Home Hub and cloud storage.
assumptions: Network traffic can be monitored

title: Extended video data retention
description: Video clips may be stored in cloud storage longer than functionally needed, increasing privacy risks over time as data accumulates.
assumptions: Retention policies may not align with functional requirements

title: Data accessible to cloud provider
description: Video data is made accessible to the cloud storage provider as a predetermined party, which may have access beyond what is functionally necessary for storage.
assumptions: Cloud provider has technical access to stored data

title: Unawareness of video recording and upload
description: Individuals captured in camera footage may be unaware that their video data is being recorded by the Home Hub and uploaded to cloud storage for processing and storage.
assumptions: People in camera view may not know they are being recorded

title: Lack of control over video data erasure
description: Data subjects may lack control to rectify or erase their video data from cloud storage, particularly if retention policies are not transparent or configurable.
assumptions: Data subject rights implementation may be limited

title: Potential storage limitation violation
description: Video data stored in cloud storage may be retained longer than necessary for the stated purpose, potentially violating storage limitation principles under GDPR and similar regulations.
assumptions: Retention periods may not be aligned with functional needs

title: Sensitive motion data collected
description: Motion alert data reveals presence and movement patterns within the home, which is highly sensitive personal data that may exceed what is functionally required for simple alert notification.
assumptions: Motion data includes timestamp and location within home that reveals occupancy patterns

title: Linking through unique identifiers in transit
description: The motion alert flow likely contains unique identifiers (device ID, user ID, home ID) that can be used to link this data to a specific individual or household during transmission.
assumptions: Motion alerts include identifying information to route to correct user

title: Observed communications reveal activity
description: Network monitoring of the motion alert transmission could reveal when motion is detected in the home, exposing occupancy patterns to eavesdroppers.
assumptions: Data flow is observable on network without encryption or with compromised encryption

title: Profiling through motion pattern analysis
description: The mobile app backend can analyze motion alert patterns to profile when individuals are home, their daily routines, and movement behaviors within the home.
assumptions: Backend stores and analyzes motion alert history over time

title: Revealing attributes from motion data
description: Motion data contains revealing attributes (timing, frequency, location) that support identification of data subjects and their behavioral patterns.
assumptions: Motion alerts include sufficient detail to infer individual presence and behavior

title: Excessive frequency of motion data processing
description: Real-time motion alerts result in frequent processing of personal data, potentially more frequently than functionally needed for security notification purposes.
assumptions: System processes every motion event in real-time rather than batching or filtering

title: Extended retention of motion data
description: Motion alert data may be stored longer than functionally needed for the alert notification purpose, creating unnecessary privacy risk.
assumptions: Backend retains motion history for analytics or other purposes beyond immediate alerting
uncertainty_note: Retention period not specified in flow description

title: Unawareness of motion data processing
description: Data subjects may not be fully aware of how their motion data is being collected, processed, stored, or disclosed by the mobile app backend.
assumptions: Privacy notices may not clearly explain motion data processing scope

title: Lack of control over motion data preferences
description: Data subjects may lack control to set preferences or consent regarding how their motion data is processed, including frequency, retention, and secondary uses.
assumptions: System may not provide granular consent options for motion data processing

title: Violation of data minimization principle
description: Processing motion data with high frequency and detail may violate GDPR data minimization if more data is processed than actually needed for the alert functionality.
assumptions: Motion data includes more detail than necessary for simple presence notification
uncertainty_note: Depends on actual data fields in motion alert

title: Profiling through motion detection patterns
description: Motion detection notifications can be analyzed to profile the homeowner's behavior patterns, including when they are home, movement patterns within the property, and daily routines.
assumptions: The backend processes and sends motion detection data that could be aggregated over time

title: Processing of identified homeowner data
description: The mobile app backend processes and sends notifications to a specifically identified homeowner, requiring their identity to be known and processed.
assumptions: The system must identify which homeowner to send notifications to

title: Identifier in notification data
description: The notification likely contains unique identifiers (user ID, device ID, account ID) to route the motion alert to the correct homeowner's phone.
assumptions: Notifications require routing identifiers to reach the correct recipient

title: Detection through observed communications
description: The transmission of motion detection notifications reveals that motion was detected at the homeowner's property, which could be observed by network monitoring or interception.
assumptions: The data flow could be monitored or intercepted

title: Sensitive motion detection data disclosure
description: Motion detection data reveals occupancy and movement patterns, which are sensitive personal data types that disclose when the homeowner is present or absent from their property.
assumptions: Motion detection data is considered sensitive personal data

title: Implicit disclosure of occupancy status
description: Motion detection notifications implicitly disclose whether the homeowner is home or away, which is personal data collected as a side-effect of the explicit motion detection functionality.
assumptions: Motion detection inherently reveals occupancy information

title: Unawareness of motion data processing
description: Homeowners may not be fully aware of how their motion detection data is processed, stored, or what inferences can be drawn from notification patterns.
assumptions: Users may not understand the full implications of motion detection notifications

title: Lack of control over notification preferences
description: Homeowners may lack granular control over what motion detection data triggers notifications, how frequently they receive them, or what data is processed to generate alerts.
assumptions: Notification settings may not offer sufficient customization options

title: Sensitive device-usage analytics shared
description: Device-usage analytics can reveal sensitive behavioral patterns, location data, app usage habits, and other personal information that may be more sensitive than functionally required for analytics purposes.
assumptions: Device-usage analytics typically contain behavioral and usage pattern data that can be considered sensitive personal data.

title: Data shared with external vendor
description: Personal data is made accessible to an external cloud analytics vendor (EE3), increasing exposure beyond what might be functionally necessary for the mobile app's core functionality.
assumptions: The cloud analytics vendor is a predetermined external party with whom data is shared.

title: Users unaware of third-party analytics sharing
description: Data subjects may not be aware that their device-usage analytics are being shared with a third-party cloud analytics vendor, as this sharing may not be clearly disclosed in privacy notices.
assumptions: Third-party data sharing is often buried in privacy policies or not prominently disclosed to users.

title: Lack of user control over analytics sharing
description: Users may lack the ability to set preferences or consent regarding how their device-usage analytics are processed and shared with the cloud analytics vendor.
assumptions: Analytics sharing is often enabled by default with limited opt-out mechanisms.

title: Invalid consent for third-party data sharing
description: Personal data collection and processing for sharing with the cloud analytics vendor may not rely on valid, informed consent, particularly if consent is bundled or not specific to this third-party sharing.
assumptions: Third-party analytics sharing often occurs without granular, informed consent.

title: Device identifiers transmitted in analytics
description: The analytics data flow may contain unique device identifiers or user identifiers that enable linking of data to specific individuals across different contexts.
assumptions: Analytics data often includes device IDs, user IDs, or similar unique identifiers for tracking purposes.
uncertainty_note: Uncertain whether 'aggregated' data truly excludes identifiers.

title: Quasi-identifiers in aggregated analytics
description: Even aggregated analytics data may contain combinations of attributes (usage patterns, timestamps, device types) that serve as quasi-identifiers enabling identification of individuals.
assumptions: Aggregated data can still contain quasi-identifying information when combined with other datasets.

title: Individual profiling by analytics vendor
description: The cloud analytics vendor can analyze device-usage patterns to profile individuals, linking data to specific users based on behavioral patterns and usage characteristics.
assumptions: Analytics vendors typically perform profiling and behavioral analysis on collected data.

title: Data enrichment and analysis beyond original purpose
description: The cloud analytics vendor may further treat, analyze, and enrich the device-usage data in ways not necessary for the original analytics purpose, potentially creating additional privacy risks.
assumptions: Analytics vendors typically enrich and analyze data for their own business purposes beyond the original collection intent.

title: Extended data retention by vendor
description: The cloud analytics vendor may retain device-usage analytics data longer than functionally needed, potentially indefinitely, without clear retention policies aligned with data subject expectations.
assumptions: Third-party vendors often retain data longer than the original collecting service.

title: Video content reveals homeowner identity and activities
description: The video clip contains revealing attributes including the homeowner's appearance, activities, home layout, and potentially other individuals present. This identifiable information is processed by the mobile app backend when retrieving the video for playback.
assumptions: Video content typically contains visual information that can identify the data subject and their activities

title: Video analysis enables profiling of homeowner behavior
description: The mobile app backend could analyze video content to derive patterns about the homeowner's daily routines, habits, presence patterns, and lifestyle, enabling behavioral profiling.
assumptions: Video content can be analyzed for behavioral patterns and the backend has capability to perform such analysis

title: Video is highly sensitive personal data
description: Video footage is considered highly sensitive personal data as it captures visual information about individuals in their private space. The processing of such sensitive data requires strict necessity justification.
assumptions: Video content in a home security context is considered sensitive personal data under privacy regulations

title: Video retention duration may exceed functional necessity
description: The mobile app backend may process or retain video data longer than needed for the playback functionality, potentially keeping historical footage accessible beyond what is functionally required.
assumptions: Video storage and retrieval systems often retain data longer than the immediate playback requirement

title: Video evidence can attribute actions to homeowner
description: The video data can be used as evidence to attribute specific actions, presence, or activities to the homeowner, preventing them from denying certain claims about their behavior or whereabouts.
assumptions: Video footage can serve as evidentiary material for attribution purposes

title: Limited control over video data rectification and erasure
description: The homeowner may lack adequate control to rectify or erase video data that is no longer relevant or contains incorrect information, particularly if the backend retains copies or metadata.
assumptions: Video data systems may not provide robust deletion or rectification mechanisms for data subjects

title: Potential violation of data minimization principle
description: Processing full video clips for playback may involve more personal data than strictly necessary, potentially violating GDPR's data minimization principle if less intrusive alternatives exist.
assumptions: GDPR applies to this system and data minimization is a requirement
uncertainty_note: Depends on specific implementation and whether less intrusive alternatives are technically feasible
